content: Obstetric Complications and Management: 1. Malpresentation and Multiple Pregnancy: Address malpresentation (e.g., breech) and manage appropriately. For multiple pregnancies, ensure readiness for potential complications. 2. Fetal Distress: Monitor for signs of fetal distress and manage as per established protocols. 3. Obstetric Problems on Admission: Evaluate and classify any obstetric issues upon admission. Treat and provide advice based on clinical findings. 4. Specific Obstetric Risks: Be vigilant for conditions such as: Warts or keloid tissue that may obstruct delivery. History of third-degree perineal tears. Bleeding during the third trimester. Previous cesarean section or instrumental delivery (forceps/vacuum). Maternal age under 14 years, which increases the risk of complications. 5. Delivery Techniques: Perform a generous episiotomy if necessary and control the delivery of the fetal head carefully. In cases of late labor, ensure delivery is conducted with appropriate support. 6. Preterm Labor: Reassess fetal presentation, as breech is more common in preterm cases. Encourage the mother to lie on her left side if supine. Avoid routine cesarean sections for preterm births unless clinically indicated. Administer magnesium sulfate for women at risk of imminent preterm birth before 32 weeks to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy in the infant. Prepare for potential rapid delivery of a small baby and ensure neonatal resuscitation equipment is ready. 7. Rupture of Membranes: Administer appropriate IM/IV antibiotics if membranes have been ruptured for more than 18 hours. Plan for neonatal treatment as needed. 8. Dehydration: Provide oral fluids or IV fluids (1 liter over 3 hours) if the woman cannot drink. 9. HIV Management: Ensure the woman adheres to prescribed antiretroviral therapy (ART). Provide supportive care throughout labor. Supportive Care During Labor: 1. Communication: Explain all procedures, seek consent, and keep the woman informed about labor progress. Offer encouragement and reassurance, respecting her privacy and wishes. 2. Cleanliness: Encourage the woman to bathe or wash at the onset of labor. Wash the vulva and perineal area before each examination. Use clean gloves for vaginal examinations and maintain a clean birthing environment. 3. Mobility and Positioning: Encourage the woman to move freely and adopt positions of her choice during labor. Support her choice of position for delivery, such as squatting or kneeling. 4. Urination and Nutrition: Encourage frequent bladder emptying. Allow the woman to eat and drink as she wishes, emphasizing nutritious liquids. 5. Breathing Techniques: Teach the woman to focus on slow, steady breathing to manage pain and prevent hyperventilation. During the end of the first stage of labor, teach panting to avoid premature pushing. 6. Pain Relief: Suggest position changes and encourage mobility. Allow the companion to provide support, such as back massages or holding her hand. Encourage the use of warm baths or showers if available. Monitoring During Labor: 1. First Stage (Not Active Labor): Monitor every hour for emergency signs, contractions, and fetal heart rate. Check cervical dilation every 4 hours unless otherwise indicated. Record findings in the labor record and partograph. 2. First Stage (Active Labor): Monitor every 30 minutes for contractions and fetal heart rate. Record progress and ensure the woman is never left alone. 3. Second Stage (Delivery of Baby): Ensure all delivery equipment, including neonatal resuscitation tools, is ready. Assist the woman into a comfortable, upright position. Allow her to push as she wishes with contractions but do not urge her to push. If progress is delayed, reassess and consider referral or intervention. 4. Third Stage (Delivery of Placenta): Administer 10 IU oxytocin IM to promote uterine contraction. Use controlled cord traction to deliver the placenta, applying counter-traction to the uterus. If the placenta is not delivered within 30 minutes and there is no bleeding, encourage breastfeeding and repeat controlled cord traction. If bleeding occurs or the placenta is not delivered within an hour, manage as per postpartum hemorrhage protocols and consider manual removal. Immediate Newborn Care: 1. After Delivery: Place the baby on the mother’s abdomen or in her arms for skin-to-skin contact. Thoroughly dry the baby and assess breathing. If the baby is not breathing or gasping, initiate neonatal resuscitation immediately. 2. Cord Management: Clamp and cut the cord 1-3 minutes after birth, ensuring proper technique to prevent bleeding. 3. Temperature Regulation: Keep the baby warm with additional blankets if the room temperature is below 25°C. 4. Breastfeeding: Encourage early initiation of breastfeeding unless contraindicated (e.g., HIV-positive mother opting for replacement feeding). This detailed guidance ensures safe and effective management of labor, delivery, and immediate postpartum care for both the mother and the newborn.
